source.title: Momentum Steering: Activation Steering Meets Optimization
source.citation: Ryan Lee T. Z. et al.
source.authors: Ryan Lee T. Z.; Dung Viet Nguyen; Hieu M. Vu; Lei Zhang; Linh Duy Tran; Tan Minh Nguyen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplement are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper builds Momentum Steering on difference-in-means directions and evaluates its own steering-based jailbreak method. It reports attack and benchmark performance, but does not test whether the original single direction causally mediates refusal or whether existing attacks suppress it.
record.gate_note: The harmful-versus-harmless difference-in-means baseline and Momentum/Adam variants are used in Angular Steering jailbreak experiments. Those results measure the performance of these steering configurations, not the claim's specified direct projection or addition intervention. No result tests refusal induced on harmless prompts. Cited findings about refusal directions are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper uses harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means directions as candidate directions for steering and reports only how its own momentum and Adam variants change jailbreak ASR and tinyBenchmarks scores against a difference-in-means Angular Steering baseline. It never ablates the refusal direction against an unsteered control in the original manner. It does not add the direction to harmless prompts to induce refusal. It does not test weight edits, attack mechanisms, multi-direction structure, harm/refusal separation, transfer, training dependence or reasoning models. All results compare steering-vector construction methods, so this is T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that momentum- and Adam-based candidate directions give stronger, more robust steering than difference-in-means baselines, including jailbreak ASR gains and toxicity reduction, with largely preserved utility. They draw no conclusion about whether a single refusal direction mediates refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-versus-harmless difference-in-means refusal directions as the baseline, but evaluates Angular Steering and proposes momentum/Adam accumulation rather than directly testing the original single-direction projection and addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model, steering configuration, momentum coefficient, sequential versus non-sequential computation, and decoding setup. The authors report coefficient tuning may be needed; the coefficient ablation on Gemma2-9B-Instruct peaks at β = 0.95, while Gemma2-27B-Instruct's non-sequential result peaks at β = 0.99.

fits_no_version.finding: Accumulating per-layer difference-in-means refusal directions with a momentum or Adam buffer raises Angular Steering jailbreak ASR over plain difference-in-means on most models, most strongly on Gemma2. For example, Gemma2-27B rises from 4.81 to 71.15 and deeper-aligned Gemma2-9B from 1.92 to 34.62. tinyBenchmarks scores stay mostly similar. Gains depend on the momentum coefficient, and some configurations drop below baseline (Llama3.1-8B sequential AA 75.96 vs 86.54).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum-accumulated difference-in-means candidate directions make steering-based refusal bypass more effective than plain difference-in-means directions, depending on model and coefficient.

record.code_released: Source codes for experiments are stated to be provided in the supplementary materials of the paper; no URL stated.
record.problems: Attack outcomes are measured using an open-source HarmBench classifier; the core ASR tables do not report uncertainty. General utility is assessed using tinyBenchmarks rather than a broad capability evaluation, and the authors note some configuration- and coefficient-dependence.
record.rows_left_out: The 58 kept rows prioritize the main ASR comparisons (Tables 1, 3, and 7) and three tinyBenchmarks metrics for the Table 1 momentum configuration. Omitted Table 1 tinyArc and Adam utility scores; Table 2 sequential ActAdd/Directional Ablation configurations; Figure 3 reduced-dataset-size results; Table 4 toxicity-mitigation results; Tables 5 and 8 momentum-coefficient sweeps; Table 10 ActAdd results; and Table 11 top-K sampling results. These include related steering outcomes but are method/configuration extensions rather than tests of the catalogued causal claim.

untested.parts: There is no directional ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction compared with an unsteered model's refusal rate. Induced refusal on harmless prompts is not tested. Capability is not compared with an unmodified model.
Does not analyse whether existing jailbreaks suppress the direction, and no adversarial training.
Does not compare one direction with affine, cone or multi-direction accounts. The momentum-accumulated directions are an engineering variant and are not compared as a representation.
Harmfulness judgment is not separated from refusal.
Refusal training is not varied. The deeper-safety-aligned Gemma2-9B is attacked, but only to compare steering methods.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix F (Table 9) states that plain difference-in-means Angular Steering fails to jailbreak Gemma2-9B at any angle (baseline ASR 7.69%). This is incidental and not tested against the original V1 protocol. Angular Steering rotates within a plane rather than ablating a direction, and no no-steering ASR is reported. A researcher could note that plain difference-in-means steering is weak on Gemma2 models under this method, but it cannot ground a V1 verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly ablate the difference-in-means direction at every layer and position, test whether that removes refusal, or add it to harmless prompts to measure induced refusal.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Evaluates its own direction-based steering jailbreak; it does not test whether other attacks work by suppressing the direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or other transfer test of the direction.
Does not vary refusal training or its timing to test whether a removable direction forms.
